entry.title: The future of substance abuse disorder

media:group.media:title: The future of substance abuse disorder
media:group.media:description:
Keith Humphreys is an expert in substance use disorder, treatment, and drug policy whose research helped explain why fentanyl overdose deaths have dropped by a third since 2023. He laments that 10 million still die each year and millions more are incarcerated with substance use disorders. Yet he says the most harmful drugs are often the legal ones: tobacco and alcohol. For policymakers who want lasting solutions, he recommends evidence over opinion, pointing to the proven success of Alcoholics Anonymous as “the closest thing we have in public health to a free lunch.” Recently, his focus has turned to GLP-1 drugs for treating addiction. “It’s not all about the gut; these drugs clearly affect the brain,” Humphreys tells host Russ Altman on this episode of Stanford Engineering’s The Future of Everything podcast.

media:group.media:title: The future of brain development
media:group.media:description:
Live from the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute 2026 Symposium, and in partnership with the institute’s podcast From Our Neurons to Yours, host Russ Altman talks with brain development researchers Karen Parker and Jason Yeatman. Parker studies autism at the molecular level, translating those findings to clinical trials. Yeatman studies dyslexia, deploying assessment tools to 1.2 million students at nearly 3,000 schools. While their individual work is different in approach, the conversation sheds light on the similar obstacles both face in turning scientific discovery into real-world impact. Their mutual takeaway is that scientific breakthroughs are increasingly the work of diverse teams, not lone investigators. “The magic happens at the interdisciplinary boundaries,” Parker tells Altman on this episode of Stanford Engineering’s The Future of Everything podcast.

entry.title: The future of climate change beliefs

media:group.media:title: The future of climate change beliefs
media:group.media:description:
In her research, Madalina Vlasceanu explores the psychology of sustainability. She’s keenly interested in how people form beliefs and what motivates them to action. Her research shows that the erosion of institutional trust is an intentional tactic and that climate polarization is manufactured by fossil fuel interests to drive disengagement. Vlasceanu offers evidence-based recommendations for turning despair into action. Concern for future generations is an effective strategy for generating policy support, she says, while restoring trust in institutions is key to action. Climate change is a collective problem and we must address it collectively, Vlasceanu tells host Russ Altman on this episode of Stanford Engineering’s The Future of Everything podcast.
